answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line opens the Preface to the Second Edition of Jane Eyre, dated 21 December 1847 and signed “Currer Bell” — Brontë's own pseudonym. She wrote it to answer critics who accused the novel of being irreligious and immoral.

source.heading: The source

Second edition, Smith, Elder & Co., London, 1848

source.excerpt: Conventionality is not morality. Self-righteousness is not religion. To attack the first is not to assail the last. To pluck the mask from the face of the Pharisee, is not to lift an impious hand to the Crown of Thorns.
trail: Jane Eyre was first published anonymously as by “Currer Bell” on 19 October 1847; Brontë added this preface for the second edition, dated 21 December 1847.
The passage is preserved in the Wikisource transcription of the preface, which matches the Gutenberg text word for word.
A summary of the preface's argument — that challenging convention is not the same as rejecting religion — is corroborated by Victorian Web's annotated edition of the preface.

author.heading: About Charlotte Brontë
author.bio: Charlotte Brontë was the eldest of the three Brontë sisters who survived to adulthood and published Jane Eyre in October 1847 under the male pseudonym Currer Bell. The novel's frank first-person voice and its heroine's insistence on moral and emotional independence made it both a sensation and, for some critics, a scandal — prompting the defense Brontë wrote into her Preface to the Second Edition.

context.heading: Why Brontë wrote it
lead: Jane Eyre was an immediate popular success after its October 1847 publication, but some reviewers attacked it as subversive and anti-Christian in its sympathies. When Brontë prepared a second edition, she added a new preface to answer those critics directly.

In it she argues that questioning rigid social convention is not the same as attacking real morality, and that unmasking false piety is not an assault on genuine religion — the distinction captured in this line.
